plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 3: Polynomial and Rational Functions
plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a rational function on a coordinate plane and marks the two distinct ways its graph breaks. The horizontal axis is labeled x and ticked at odd values from -3 through 9; the vertical axis is ticked at even values from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid. The teal curve comes in two branches. The left branch enters from the far left almost flat and just above the x-axis, carries a small hollow open circle at x equal to -1 marking a point removed from the graph, then descends through the x-axis at x equal to 1 and drops steeply, running off the bottom of the frame as it approaches x equal to 3. The right branch begins high just to the right of x equal to 3, falls quickly, then levels off toward the right edge near y equal to 1. A red dashed vertical line stands at x equal to 3, labeled below the axis in red as Vertical asymptote at x = 3. A blue annotation at the upper left reads Removable discontinuity at x = -1, with a thin arrow to the open circle. Setting the hollow dot against the dashed line is the contrast being drawn: one break is a single missing point, the other sends the curve toward infinity on both sides.

interactionPlan.concept: A rational graph can break either by having one removable missing point or by becoming unbounded at a vertical asymptote, and these come from different algebraic causes.

interactions.label: Highlight break type
interactions.teaches: A removable discontinuity is a single missing point on an otherwise continuous branch, while a vertical asymptote is a place where the graph grows without bound

interactions.label: Trace x near 3
interactions.teaches: As x gets close to 3, the y-value shoots downward from the left and upward from the right, so the break at x = 3 cannot be repaired by filling in one point

interactions.label: Factor-cancelled view
interactions.teaches: The hole at x = -1 comes from a cancelled factor, so the simplified curve is continuous there except that the original function still has one excluded input

demo_steps.title: Find the removable hole
demo_steps.narration: The hollow circle at x = -1 marks a point that is missing from the graph. The nearby curve behaves normally on both sides, so this break is only one absent function value.

demo_steps.title: Reveal why the hole occurs
demo_steps.narration: The common factor x + 1 cancels algebraically, leaving the same curve shape but preserving the restriction x ≠ -1. That is why the graph has a hole rather than a vertical blow-up at x = -1.

demo_steps.title: Contrast the vertical asymptote
demo_steps.narration: At x = 3, the dashed red line is not a missing point. Moving the trace point toward x = 3 shows the curve plunging downward on the left and rising upward on the right.

demo_steps.title: Approach from the right
demo_steps.narration: Just to the right of x = 3, the graph is extremely high and then falls back toward its long-run level near y = 1. This unbounded behavior is what makes x = 3 a vertical asymptote.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A cancelled factor creates a removable hole, but an uncancelled denominator zero creates a vertical asymptote where the function values become unbounded.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate a square coordinate grid with black arrowed axes, teal curve, teal open circle at approximately (-1, 0.5), and a red dashed vertical line at x = 3. The curve should resemble f(x) = ((x - 1)(x + 1)) / ((x - 3)(x + 1)), simplified to (x - 1)/(x - 3) except for the hole at x = -1: it crosses the x-axis near x = 1, drops to negative infinity as x approaches 3 from the left, rises from positive infinity just right of x = 3, and approaches horizontal level y = 1 on the right. Use blue styling for the removable discontinuity annotation and red styling for the vertical asymptote annotation. Highlighting should brighten or thicken the selected feature while dimming the other; the slider should place a trace point on the curve unless x is exactly 3, where it should show an undefined warning rather than plotting a finite point.

plan.authoredInteractions:

- Slider for x approaching 3; the learner moves a trace point toward the vertical asymptote from either side, the y-value shoots downward or upward, and it becomes clear why x = 3 is not a removable hole.

authoredContext:
Notice that x+1 is a common factor to the numerator and the denominator. The zero of this factor, x=−1, is the location of the removable discontinuity. Notice also that x–3 is not a factor in both the numerator and denominator. The zero of this factor, x=3, is the vertical asymptote. See the figure.

Graph of f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x^2-2x-3) with its vertical asymptote at x=3 and a removable discontinuity at x=-1.
